stories.headline: Rays-Brewers World Series preview, predictions, odds
stories.summary: Does Tampa Bay or Milwaukee have the edge? What's the inside intel on this Fall Classic? We've got it all covered.
stories.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers against the Tampa Bay Rays. The two No. 1 seeds in the 2026 MLB playoffs. Two franchises that have never won a World Series title.

It's time for Game 1 of the World Series, featuring a 103-win Brewers squad that just took down the two-time defending champs and a red-hot Rays club that proved itself the class of the American League -- and we're here to get you ready for all the action.

With the first pitch scheduled for 8 p.m. ET at American Family Field, it's time to break down the players and matchups that matter most for both teams. We also asked our ESPN MLB experts to make their picks for who will win the Series, how many games it will take and who will be the MVP of this Fall Classic.

Note: Bradford Doolittle's World Series probabilities come from a formula that uses power ratings as the basis for 10,000 simulations to determine the most likely outcomes.

Jump to: Odds | Brewers | Rays | Predictions

World Series winner probabilities

Milwaukee Brewers

Chance of winning: 59.1% | DraftKings odds: -160

What's on the line for the Brewers: The first World Series title in franchise history -- after 57 seasons in Milwaukee. Completing the final step in the process that has seen the Brewers make the playoffs in eight of the past nine seasons and win the most games in the majors in the regular season in both 2025 and 2026.

Confirmation that they can win it all their way: Reasonably low payroll, mostly homegrown players, with speed and defense on the position-player side of things and power pitching up and down the entire staff. Affirmation that you can still win a World Series without having to sign expensive free agents. -- David Schoenfield

Three reasons Milwaukee can win:

The Brewers' bullpen is spectacular: Over 40⅔ postseason innings, the Milwaukee relievers have a 1.33 ERA, allowing just 22 hits and 14 walks, with 38 strikeouts. Aaron Ashby is having one of the best postseason performances ever, with 12⅓ scoreless innings. And because the Brewers dominated the Dodgers and quickly closed the NLCS, this group will have a week of rest going into the World Series.
Milwaukee hitters typically generate strong, competitive at-bats, embodied by Jake Bauers' 12- and 11-pitch plate appearances in the NLCS. The Rays need length from their starting pitchers if they're going to win the World Series, and that will be a challenge in the face of the deep and talented Brewers lineup.
The Brewers defense is solid. The Rays may create more chaos than any team in the big leagues, especially when they're playing in Tropicana Field, in how they bunt, in how they run the bases, and because of the presence of Chandler Simpson. But Milwaukee is a good defensive team capable of playing clean games, and only one team surrendered fewer stolen bases than the Brewers during the regular season. William Contreras vs. Simpson is one of the more intriguing matchups in this series. -- Buster Olney

Where the Brewers are vulnerable: To beat the Brewers, you have to take advantage of their starting rotation. It begins with running up the pitch counts of their two front-line starters, Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. The Dodgers actually did a good job of making those two work in Games 1 and 2 of the NLCS, getting them both out before the end of the fifth inning. The problem was they couldn't cash in on run-scoring opportunities.

The Brewers' starting options beyond Misiorowski and Henderson are relatively uninspiring, a list composed of Robert Gasser, Dustin May and Shane Drohan. Brewers manager Pat Murphy will want to rely more heavily on his bullpen in Games 3 and 4. If the Rays can tax those high-leverage arms early in this series, they'll be in good shape. Also, the more looks their hitters can get against the likes of Ashby, Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill, the better off they'll be.

But make no mistake: scoring early will be a must for the Rays. -- Alden Gonzalez

How the Brewers can pitch Junior Caminero: There was an ongoing conversation in the last series that Caminero had trouble with high fastballs. That makes some sense since his swing plane is steeper than average in order to lift the ball when he puts it in play, so a flat fastball at the top of the zone doesn't intersect with his bat path; a sinker at the bottom of the zone would match his swing plane much better.

His regular season miss rates and damage heat map shows that his misses cluster well above the zone, clear chases, but he does plenty of damage just inside and just above the top of the strike zone and lots of damage if you miss below that spot in center-cut locations. So, you don't want to go to this well that often. A steady diet of breaking stuff off the plate low and away, then high fastballs above the zone when he starts to lean over the plate should work if he chases. If Caminero can lay off those pitches, then you're really in trouble. -- Kiley McDaniel

Jeff Passan's inside intel:

After a 103-win regular season and definitive sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, there is one bit of unanimity among all types of evaluators: They love watching the Milwaukee Brewers play baseball.

"They're just a damn good team," one analyst said.

"It's a 1980s team with 2020s sensibilities," a veteran scout said.

"I wish we played like them," said a GM.

The plaudits are earned. The Brewers' style is substantive. They do little things well, and they do big things well -- or at least well enough. They impose themselves.

"They are very talented pests," another scout said.

The Rays are changeup specialists, and the Brewers will be at their best if they can hit them better than Tampa Bay's other opponents. One thing that bodes well for Milwaukee: It had the lowest chase rate on out-of-zone changeups in the big leagues, which isn't altogether surprising since their chase rate on all pitches during the regular season was the lowest.

"I want to see what they do with changeups in the zone," one analyst said. "They're going to be hunting them."

Whether they get them is another question. Of the 315 changeups Rays pitchers have thrown, only 41% were in the strike zone. Aside from one player on one night -- Ben Rice in Game 2 of the division series -- nobody has gotten an extra-base hit on an in-zone Rays changeup, and opponents are hitting .192 against it. It's a real weapon, and the Brewers -- who are 7 for 21 with one homer on in-zone changeups this postseason -- need not fall prey to it.

The most bullish Brewers backers think they're going to have a 2018 Red Sox-like finish and plow through the Rays. When pressed for a weakness, they pointed to the Brewers' infield defense as a sneaky issue.
"They make more mistakes than the Rays," one scout said, pointing to the division series in which Milwaukee made five infield errors. He also noted that of their three NLCS errors, two were by starter Logan Henderson and none by an infielder.

Shortstop Cooper Pratt played a clean NLCS after a fielding error and a pair of throwing errors against the Padres. "He's still a rookie starting at shortstop for a team that's never won a World Series," the scout said.

Another evaluator saw a different potential opportunity for Tampa Bay on the left side of Milwaukee's infield.

"Their third basemen play so deep, I'd be interested in seeing what a few bunts would do," he said, noting the contrast with Rays third baseman Junior Caminero, who is regularly positioned well into the infield grass.

One matchup an analyst is excited to see: Brewers uber-reliever Aaron Ashby vs. Tampa Bay's Ryan Vilade. Ashby is the fireballing left-handed multi-inning throwback -- figuratively and as a descriptor of his high-slot arm swing. Vilade is the Rays' right-handed specialist to combat nasty lefties who will be strategically deployed by manager Kevin Cash.
"Vilade can hit hard sinkers," he said. "I want to know if he can hit an Aaron Ashby sinker."

Tampa Bay Rays
Chance of winning: 40.1% | DraftKings odds: +140

What's on the line for the Rays: In their 29th season in Tampa Bay, the first World Series title in franchise history. Completing the final step in a long run of success -- World Series appearances in 2008 and 2020, 10 90-win seasons since and 10 playoff appearances since 2008, the best record in the American League in 2026.

Confirmation that they can win their way: Low payroll, defense, speed, small ball, finding and developing players acquired from other organizations -- like Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Drew Rasmussen. Affirmation that you can still win a World Series without having to sign expensive free agents. -- Schoenfield

Three reasons Tampa Bay can win:

Constant pressure. The Rays led the majors in contact rate and posted the lowest strikeout rate during the regular season. They bunt more than everyone else and they swipe bags whenever possible. That fusion produces relentless pressure on their opposition. They force teams to play clean baseball, a test that the Yankees in the ALDS and the Guardians in the ALCS failed at crucial points in their respective series.
Nobody embodies their brand of baseball more than Chandler Simpson, who, despite never hitting a home in the majors, bats in the middle of Tampa Bay's lineup. Simpson was one of seven qualified batters in the majors to finish with a .300 batting average this season. Perhaps the fastest player in baseball, he is a constant threat to bunt for a hit and a demon on the basepaths. His game is wreaking havoc. That's Rays baseball.

Los Tres Pequeños. Most of the Rays' thump lies with their three best hitters: Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz, and Jonathan Aranda. The Rays ranked 22nd in the majors with 169 home runs during the regular season. Their big three -- or, as manager Kevin Cash jokingly calls them, Los Tres Pequeños, Spanish for The Three Little Ones -- combined for 86 of them.
Each contributed in a major way in the ALCS. Díaz went 9-for-27 with two home runs, including a two-run shot in Game 6, with a 1.061 OPS. Aranda, after starting the series 0-for-11, collected five hits between Games 4 and 5. Caminero, the team's 23-year-old star third baseman, rebounded from earlier struggles with two hits in Game 6, including a crucial two-run homer that he celebrated with a 38.7-second trot around the bases.

The Rays can score in different ways, but slugging is the surest way to win in October. If their sluggers slug, they're tough to beat.

Starting pitching. The Rays have the best pitcher of the postseason (Drew Rasmussen), the ALCS MVP (Freddy Peralta), and an All-Star at the end of a career year (Nick Martinez) leading their starting rotation. Their four starters -- Griffin Jax is their No. 4 -- have combined for a 1.98 ERA in the playoffs, the best among the 12 participants.
Rasmussen has logged at least six innings in each of his three starts. Peralta has allowed two runs in his four outings, which includes a two-out relief appearance in Game 4 of the ALCS. Martinez allowed one run over 5⅓ innings in Game 4 before Peralta relieved him. The Rays will need length from their rotation, especially their top three, to avoid overexposing the bullpen and win this series. -- Jorge Castillo

Where the Rays are vulnerable: The only potential weakness on the Rays comes in the middle of their bullpen. Subtract closer Bryan Baker's seven scoreless innings and the rest of Tampa's bullpen has a 4.70 ERA this postseason.

If the Brewers can elevate pitch counts of the Rays' starters, they'll be able to get to the underbelly of that Rays pen. That bodes well in a best-of-seven series as it's harder to hide arms -- in fact seeing them multiple times will only benefit Milwaukee. -- Jesse Rogers

How the Rays can attack Jacob Misiorowski: As you probably guess, this is no easy task. With his fastball, Miz tends to pitch up and away from righties, and his breaking stuff is aimed low and away, for tunneling purposes. The damage against those two groups of pitches comes when they're in mistake locations: a breaking ball backs up, in the zone on the inner half or a fastball misses its spot, basically in that same spot. In two playoff starts, roughly 10% of his pitches went into this zone and a third of those were fouled off.

The game plan is to stay alive long enough so when he makes 5-10 pitches that are "mistakes" (remember: His stuff is still the best in baseball) you're swinging and not fouling it off. The bad news? The three pitches in that zone that were put in play in the playoffs were all groundouts to shortstop. -- Kiley McDaniel

Jeff Passan's inside intel:

The biggest vulnerability in the series is Tampa Bay against high-velocity fastballs. And nobody throws high-velocity fastballs like the Brewers. During the regular season, Milwaukee threw the most fastballs in the NL and third-most in MLB at 52.4%, with an average of four-seamer at 96 mph and sinker at 95.6. This postseason, they have upped their usage -- and significantly upped their velocity. The average Brewers four-seam fastball this postseason is 98.3 mph. The sinker is 97.1. Together, they comprise 56.2% of Milwaukee's pitches thrown this postseason.
During the regular season Tampa Bay had the 29th-ranked OPS against 98-mph-plus fastballs. "They're going to see a lot of fastballs, and they know it," one scout said. "Which is going to make the offspeed even more dangerous. They will chase." The hard stuff is coming in spades in Game 1 against Jacob Misiorowski, who has upped his usage from 63.3% to 67% and his velocity from 100.6 to 101 over 8⅓ innings.

One of the most interesting developments of this season, and particularly this postseason, are suggestions that the fastball's demise has, at least temporarily, reversed. Once more, velo is king.

Getting Junior Caminero's first postseason home run in the ALCS clincher was a good sign for the Rays. "They need to hit a few home runs," one scout said. "The Dodgers got beat because they got outhomered seven to one."
The Rays hit 15 more home runs than Milwaukee during the regular season, when the Brewers ranked 29th. They've turned up their power in big moments as they stomped through the NL playoffs. But Caminero is an ever-present threat, Yandy Díaz has immense power and Jonathan Aranda can go deep.

"Victor Mesa Jr. is their one guy who can really catch up to fastballs," one scout said. "If he has a big series, that could be the thing they need to win it."

The evaluators bullish on the Rays all cite the same thing, summarized well by one scout.
"Their rotation is better, and they will kill you if you make mistakes."

With Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta, Griffin Jax and Nick Martinez, the Rays offer a variety of looks, arm angles, arsenals. The only thing all of them do similarly is throw changeups 25% or so of the time. They're all capable of pitching deep into games and allowing the Rays to use only their most reliable relievers.

The Rays feast on mistakes because they don't make many themselves. They went errorless in the ALCS and have committed just one all postseason. They have stolen a postseason-best 11 bases and haven't been caught.

"You have to play the game at their speed," one scout said. "They play fast but under control both on the bases and defensively."

One scout noted the decline in closer Bryan Baker's fastball this year. He was regularly sitting 97 mph-plus through the All-Star break. Since then, it has fluctuated, going as low as 92.5 and sparingly averaging 96. Baker pitched four times in the ALCS. The hardest fastball he threw was 95.2 mph. In Game 4, every heater was in the 92s. His two fastballs in the clincher were 92.3 and 93.3. Because Baker's changeup is so devastating, it might not matter. But the Brewers know. "They're going to sit changeup on Baker," the scout said, "until he shows the velocity again."

Our predictions

Milwaukee Brewers (12 votes)
Voters: Jorge Castillo, Tristan Cockcroft, Bradford Doolittle, Alden Gonzalez, Eric Karabell, Tim Keown, Tim Kurkjian, Kiley McDaniel, Dan Mullen, Buster Olney, Jeff Passan, Jesse Rogers

In how many games? Seven games (7 votes), Six games (5 votes)

MVP: Jackson Chourio (3 votes), William Contreras (3 votes), Brice Turang (3 vote), Jacob Misiorowski (1 vote), Jake Bauers (1 vote), Garrett Mitchell (1 vote)

Tampa Bay Rays (3 votes)
Voters: Doug Glanville, Paul Hembekides, David Schoenfield

In how many games? Six games (2 votes), Seven games (1 vote)

MVP: Jonathan Aranda (1 vote), Yandy Diaz (1 vote), Drew Rasmussen (1 vote)

Explaining our picks
The Brewers were our consensus choice. Why did you pick Milwaukee?

As with the Dodgers' last year, when I had it roughly 60-40 in favor of L.A. -- similar to this year's probabilities that favor Milwaukee -- it's hard for me to pick against that strong of a projection.

At the same time, we know that even a seven-game series is far too small of a sample to ensure that the better team will win, so you do need to justify yourself with some matchup-specific observations. With this pairing, it's not hard for me to do that when picking the Brewers.

The teams are similar in big ways but different in the smaller things that add up to those big things and in a way that I ultimately think favors the Brewers. The Rays are good at everything, but the Brewers are as well, and everything Tampa Bay does well, Milwaukee is a little better. Except for bunting, that is, but as I wrote elsewhere, if the Rays are baseball's bunting juggernaut, the team right behind them is Milwaukee.

The rotation edge the Rays enjoyed over the Yankees and Guardians shouldn't be as acute in the World Series. We haven't seen the best of Jacob Misiorowski so far, and while he has been out of sorts with his command, I still think he has enough left to enjoy at least one signature outing. If it's Game 1, then that doesn't bode well for the Rays if they face him again, familiarity-related trends aside. If Misiorowski brings his A-game twice in the series, that's two Brewers wins, no matter who the Rays have starting.

The Brewers also know Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta well, as both pitched for Milwaukee. Call it a hunch, but I think this will give the Brewers an edge, whether it comes to picking up tells or whatever. Sure, Rasmussen and Peralta have been executing so well that it might not matter, but I don't see their run continuing at the same pace against Milwaukee.

Finally, the Milwaukee offense is just better by a good margin. These teams both have great outfield defenses but that may not show up much against the offenses with the two lowest average launch angles, according to TruMedia. But the Brewers' infield defense is as good as its outfield defense, while the Rays' infielders are less accomplished.

The Rays' pitching staff might not issue walks at the rate where the Brewers' lineup typically feasts, but Milwaukee can adjust to a more aggressive style and score with their combination of contact hitting, high BABIP and baserunning. Milwaukee also hits the ball harder more consistently and for more extra bases. I just see more pathways for the Brewers to score than for the Rays.

The Series is not a blowout, by any stretch. But I see the Brewers as the definitive favorite and I'm picking them to win in six. -- Doolittle

And why do you think the Rays will win it all?

The Brewers, coming off their sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are understandably sizable favorites in this World Series, but the underdog Rays match up well in two key areas that could lead to an upset.

First, the Rays put the ball in play, posting the lowest strikeout rate in the majors in the regular season. Their two top hitters, Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, both struck out below the league average rate, with Diaz fanning just 14.3% of the time, a top-25 mark among qualified hitters. Chandler Simpson was the second toughest hitter to whiff and Liam Hicks, who hasn't done much in the postseason but had an .801 OPS between the Marlins and Rays, was the seventh-toughest hitter to strike out.

Caminero did have some strikeout issues in the ALCS but got going in the final three games with three balls scorched at 106-plus mph plus a home run in Game 6. He'll need a big series but is equipped to handle Milwaukee's power staff: He had the sixth-highest OPS in the majors against pitches of 97-plus mph, hitting .339 with five home runs. The second highest OPS? Hicks.

Second, the Rays throw strikes, the perfect counterattack to the Brewers' patient approach on offense. The Rays' pitchers had the lowest walk rate in the regular season -- and the second-highest rate of first-pitch strikes. The Brewers have a very specific approach to their offensive strategy. With the bases empty, they're not trying to hit home runs -- they're trying to get on base and start the chaos. They had the lowest home run rate in the majors with the bases empty. With runners in scoring position, they still draw their walks, but they go for a little more power, improving their home run rate to 16th.

We saw this approach work against the Dodgers, as they drew 18 walks in four games and hit seven home runs (although six of their seven home runs were solo shots). But the Rays will present a different challenge. The first-pitch cat-and-mouse game will be fascinating. Will the Brewers' hitters continue to try to work the counts in their favor or get more aggressive if the Rays are pounding the zone?

One final reason to like the Rays: Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta are on a roll right now. Rasmussen allowed three runs in his three postseason starts while averaging seven innings per outing -- thus helping to limit the innings of the bullpen. Contrast that with Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski, who couldn't get through five innings in either of his two playoff starts. Peralta, meanwhile, has allowed two runs in his three starts. Logan Henderson, Milwaukee's No. 2 starter, has also failed to pitch deeper into games.

The Brewers don't even have a No. 4 starter, going with a bullpen game in the fourth game of the NLCS. This bullpen-heavy approach worked out since that series was a sweep (indeed, Brewers relievers have been credited with all seven of their postseason wins), but the longer the World Series goes, the more likely that Milwaukee bullpen wears down and the advantage switches to the Rays. We saw how Rays hitters started doing more damage against a very good Cleveland bullpen later in that series -- Caminero, Diaz and Jonathan Aranda hit .385 with three home runs and 10 RBIs over the final three games.

Look for that to happen again -- and for the Rays to win the World Series. -- Schoenfield

stories.headline: United States Grand Prix 2026: Race start time in Austin, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1's original night race is back as drivers prepare for the ultimate challenge around the Marina Bay Circuit in Singapore.
stories.body:
Formula 1 heads to Texas for the United States Grand Prix, with the championship battle set to heat up at the Circuit of the Americas.

Max Verstappen claimed his second victory this season after winning the Singapore Grand Prix for the first time.

Kimi Antonelli continued to extend his lead in the title championship to 102 points from Mercedes teammate George Russell, and there is a mathematical chance he will be able to clinch the title in Austin.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 18th round.

- Rafael Câmara to Haas: How F1's next rookie could shake up Ferrari's future

- F1 still planning Middle East finale amid Kimi Antonelli title uncertainty - sources

- Franco Colapinto urges fans to stop 'attacking' Formula 1 drivers on social media

United States Grand Prix schedule
All times in BST

Friday, October 23

Practice One: 6.30 p.m. - 7.30 p.m.

Practice Two: 10 p.m. - 11 p.m.

Saturday, October 24

Final Practice: 6.30 p.m. - 7.30 p.m.

Qualifying: 10 p.m. - 11 p.m.

Sunday, October 25

United States Grand Prix: 8 p.m. (GMT)

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the United States Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Circuit of the Americas

The Circuit of the Americas first hosted the United States Grand Prix in 2012, to mark the end of a five year wait since the race at Indianapolis.

Mario Andretti, who won the world championship in 1978, opened the track and it has become a popular race among drivers and fans alike with plenty of overtaking action and drama.

COTA is a varied circuit with straights, esses through to sector two, and a series of hair-pins in sector three. The high-speed corners takes some inspiration from Silverstone and Hockenheim.

It's a mix of fast corners, long straights and has one of the steepest elevation climbs to Turn 1.

United States Grand Prix

Circuit: Circuit of the Americas; Austin, Texas

Previous winners in United States

2014: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2015: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2016: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2017: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2018: Kimi Räikkönen (Ferrari)

2019: Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes)

2021: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024: Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2025: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2012

Lap record: 1:36.169, Charles Leclerc (2019)

Laps: 56 laps of 5.5km

Most wins: Lewis Hamilton with six (2007, 2012, 2014-2017) Other winners from the current grid are Verstappen (2021-2023, 2025) and Leclerc (2024).

Most poles: Hamilton (2007, 2016-2018) is tied with Michael Schumacher (2000-2002, 2006) on four. Other pole sitters from the current grid are Verstappen (2021 and 2025), Carlos Sainz (2022), Leclerc (2023) and Lando Norris (2024).

Weather forecast

The weather for the United States Grand Prix is expected to be light rain with a gentle breeze throughout the course of the weekend, with highs of 32°C.

What happened last time out?
Verstappen edged out Norris to take an imperious pole position by 0.291 seconds.

The Red Bull driver dominated the race and posed as a serious threat to McLaren's Norris and Oscar Piastri in the drivers' championship.

Norris finished second and cut his lead to 14 points to Piastri in the standings, who finished fifth. Verstappen ended the weekend only 40 points behind Piastri with five races left of the season.

Who will win this year?

Antonelli will be as focused as ever to claim his ninth victory of the season with one hand already on the drivers' championship trophy.

However, Mercedes are still working on how to best optimise its current upgrade package. Last time out in Singapore, the team ran Russell on the older specification, while Antonelli had the upgraded package.

Red Bull were labelled by rivals as the "team to beat" for the remaining six races of the season. There seems to be no stopping Verstappen, who has won the U.S. Grand Prix four times.

Don't count out Hamilton who holds the record for six wins around COTA and will be looking to get his seventh podium for Ferrari this season.

stories.headline: How former Chicago Sky stars found new homes in Golden State, Atlanta
stories.summary: Two of the Finals' biggest stars were first-round picks from the Chicago Sky -- who traded both away.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- The in-house public address announcer at State Farm Arena used the pregame introductions to officially cement the newest moniker for Angel Reese, who made her postseason Atlanta debut with another record-setting performance Wednesday in Game 3 of the WNBA Finals. Fans delighted as their "Queen of the South" hopped off the bench and proceeded to confound the visiting Golden State Valkyries for the next 40 minutes.

Four days earlier, and 2,100 miles away, the decibels echoed throughout Chase Center in San Francisco as the final buzzer sounded in Game 1. Chants of "Gab-by! Gab-by! Gab-by!" made it difficult to hear any conversation as the sellout crowd of 18,064 clad in violet strained its vocal cords after the Valkyries' victory. Gabby Williams was Ballhalla's heroine.

Reese and Williams are the leaders of their respective teams after moving to new franchises last offseason. Both took unusual paths at arriving in environments that seem tailor-made for them after beginning their careers as first-round draft picks in Chicago and leaving after the relationships turned acrimonious. A change of scenery was facilitated, and the pair have thrived.

"I think it's good to take a step back from those moments and appreciate where you are," Williams said. "Even before this year, I was always very thankful for what happened to me with Chicago, and I've never looked at that moment with spite. I've always looked at that moment as the turning point of my career, and always just been really thankful that it went that way. ...

"I wouldn't change anything about where I'm at in my career right now. I'm exactly where I need to be."

REESE'S FINALS HAVE been nothing short of historic. After the Dream went down 0-1 in San Francisco, she demanded the ball in Game 2 -- and led the way with 30 points and 16 rebounds, joining Jonquel Jones and Breanna Stewart as the only players in Finals history with a 30 and 15 game. In a Game 3 win, she became the youngest WNBA player to record a double-double in her first three Finals contests.

It would have been difficult to imagine a year ago. Six months ago, Reese was still a member of the Chicago Sky. After the team drafted her No. 7 in 2024, Reese was named an All-Star, made the All-Rookie team, led the league in rebounding and set the WNBA record for most consecutive double-doubles at 15. She missed the last six games of her rookie season with a wrist injury, and the team missed the playoffs. Then-coach Teresa Weatherspoon, who Reese was close with, was fired after one season. In Reese's second season, she was named an All-Star and led the league in rebounds again -- but then everything imploded.

Never one to hold her tongue, she told the Chicago Tribune in September 2025 that she wouldn't settle "for the same s--- we did this year" and that the team "[has] to get great players" during the offseason, or she would consider making a future change. The Sky suspended her for the first half against the Las Vegas Aces on Sept. 7, 2025, for "comments detrimental to the team." Being on the injury list with a back issue for the final games of the season, she never played again for the franchise.

For someone who won four high school championships and an NCAA title, going 23-61 in her first two WNBA seasons brought frustration. Still, in December 2025, Reese -- who had two more years on her rookie deal -- said she planned to remain with the Sky, noting that she was still under contract. The Sky added talent going into the 2026 season, but a week before the WNBA draft, they traded Reese to the Dream for two first-round picks. Jaws dropped around the league when the trade was announced.

"To be able to get a player of Angel's talent in Year 3 when you didn't draft them is really unique and special," Dream general manager Dan Padover told ESPN. "Because of how much time is left in her career, and someone of that magnitude. Sometimes you're getting [them in their] late 20s, early 30s, but to get her at 24 was really, really good for us."

In 2026, Reese was named an All-Star for the third straight season, won the rebounding title for a third consecutive campaign and helped Atlanta reach the Finals for the first time since 2013. She averaged 16.4 points, 12.1 rebounds, 2.8 assists, 1.8 steals and was a deterrent at the rim, earning her Defensive Player of the Year award. Reese was one of just two players to average a double-double for the season.

Padover worked his magic again with the late-season signing of DeWanna Bonner after the league's all-time No. 3 scorer was waived by the Phoenix Mercury to enable Bonner to go to a contender. Padover pounced.

"I went right to Dan and told him that he was the greatest ever," Dream guard Shatori Walker-Kimbrough said. "I'm like, how do you keep doing this? Who allows this?"

Reese has spoken about how comfortable she is in Atlanta. She and coach Karl Smesko formed a bond where he can push her out of her comfort zone. During a training camp practice, Smesko paused everything and wouldn't resume the session until Reese knocked down consecutive 3-pointers. He wanted her to get used to taking the shot with confidence when all eyes are on her, not just working alone on the side. Reese trusted that the moment was for her benefit -- even if she didn't like it.

"I didn't want to feel embarrassed of how long it could have taken me to make them," Reese said. "But it's a coach that really believes in you and he knows what's best."

Smesko added, "I can remember her being mad at me."

But that relationship and the one formed with teammates has allowed to Reese to flourish.

"When they pour into your players and all you have to do is come to work and think about basketball, I think that makes everything easy," Reese said. "The coaches really care about you genuinely, not just as basketball players, but as people. Anything you need, they have for you."

WILLIAMS WAS THE No. 4 pick by the Sky in 2018 in a talented draft that included A'ja Wilson, Kelsey Mitchell, Jordin Canada, Azura Stevens and Ariel Atkins. The two-time All-Star would last three seasons in the Windy City -- a divorce that would stem from a loss of trust.

Williams was determined to play for France in the Olympics in 2021, her first opportunity for the senior national team. Representing France has always been a priority for Williams -- her mother is French, she holds dual citizenship and grew up speaking French with her grandmother.

That dedication drove a wedge between her and the team that drafted her. Williams believed her plans was understood by the organization when she missed training camp in 2021, but the Sky suspended her for the season. Williams responded with a trade request, and she was acquired by the Los Angeles Sparks in May 2021 but never played for them since she spent the season playing for the French national team. The Sparks traded her in February 2022 to the Seattle Storm, where she became a three-time All-Defense selection.

That development, plus more international success, made her an absolute priority for the Valkyries as they went into their second season. "Her killer mode goes up a level every game," Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase said. "The best thing she told me, 'Just go at me. Just go directly at me. In games, I need directness.' I'm like, don't be saying that if you don't want it. Those are the best players to coach because there's no B.S."

Coming off her first All-Star appearance in 2025, Williams had her best year in her first season with the Valkyries. She averaged 14.4 points, 3.3 rebounds, 2.2 assists and 1.6 steals and was the Defensive Player of the Year runner-up. Williams proved to be the additional player to lift Golden State -- a team built without the traditional superstar model -- into the Finals, only a year after it became the first expansion franchise to make the playoffs.

"Sometimes it's just like trusting what the universe gives you," Williams said. "It's easy for me to come to work, and that goes a long way. When you're just surrounded by people who enjoy being around each other, who enjoy being in a certain environment, it's really easy."

The bottom line is fit matters. On and off the court, Reese and Willliams went through their own journeys to end up in places that appear to be ideal situations. And in their new homes, both unlocked another level of their talents with career years.

"Right place, right time, I think is definitely what I would attribute to Gabby's success right now," Golden State general manager Ohemma Nyanin said.

stories.headline: NHL Power Rankings: Fantasy hockey pickups for all 32 teams
stories.summary: The Hurricanes hang on to the No. 1 spot, with some major jumbles in the poll thereafter.
stories.body:
Another week, another No. 1 spot in our poll for the defending Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes. But while there was no change at the top, there were substantial changes from Nos. 2 to 32 this week.

Plus, do you need help maximizing your fantasy hockey team's chances?

You're in luck, because Sean Allen (Eastern Conference) and Victoria Matiash (Western Conference) are here to identify one worthwhile pickup for all 32 clubs.

And a reminder: It's not too late to play ESPN Fantasy Hockey, with new leagues starting every Monday.

How we rank: A panel of ESPN hockey commentators, analysts, reporters and editors sends in a 1-32 poll based on the games through Wednesday. Those ballots are combined to come up with the rankings you see below.

Note: Previous ranking for each team refers to the previous edition, published on Oct. 16. Points percentages are through Thursday's games.

1. Carolina Hurricanes
Previous ranking: 1

Points percentage: 75%

Jaccob Slavin, D, (1.67 fantasy points per game, 67.3% available in ESPN leagues): Slavin has 18 fantasy points without a goal or any real power-play time. That's a floor built on peripherals and a 10-6 edge at 5-on-5 for a Carolina team allowing just 22.4 shots a game. Long a real-hockey darling, he's finally paying off in fantasy, too.

Next seven days: @ STL (Oct. 24), vs. BOS (Oct. 27), vs. CBJ (Oct. 29)

2. Edmonton Oilers
Previous ranking: 3

Points percentage: 85%

Devon Levi, G (2.72 FPPG, 61.5% available): Toss out the first two games of the season under new coach Mike Babcock, and the Oilers are icing the second-best defense in the NHL. For which Levi deserves some personal credit through six appearances, as made evident by his 4.82 goals saved above expected (GSAx) metric, according to Evolving Hockey.

Next seven days: vs. TOR (Oct. 24), vs. DET (Oct. 26), vs. CGY (Oct. 28)

3. Vegas Golden Knights
Previous ranking: 2

Points percentage: 66.67%

Adin Hill, G (3.91 FPPG, 78.6% available): After stumbling through 2025-26, the Vegas netminder looks back to his old solid self. Carrying a 4-0 record and 2.21 GAA into Thursday, Hill has been better than Carter Hart to date. It might not be too long before he gets more opportunities to backstop one of the best teams in the West.

Next seven days: @ CBJ (Oct. 24), vs. OTT (Oct. 27)

4. Tampa Bay Lightning
Previous ranking: 9

Points percentage: 77.78%

Charle-Edouard D'Astous, D (1.54 FPPG, 96.8% available): D'Astous just earned a promotion worth noticing, as he has been on the ice for most of the Lightning's power-play time over the past two games. A defender with top-unit access on a contender is worth a speculative add, especially at barely 3% rostered.

Next seven days: @ COL (Oct. 23), @ UTA (Oct. 24), vs. WPG (Oct. 29)

5. Boston Bruins
Previous ranking: 7

Points percentage: 77.27%

James Hagens, C (1.94 FPPG, 86.8% available): Hagens is doing a lot with a little. The rookie is averaging under 13 minutes a night, yet he has three goals in 10 games while skating with Elias Lindholm and Casey Mittelstadt lately, and Boston has outscored opponents 7-3 at 5-on-5 with him on the ice. More ice time is the only thing missing.

Next seven days: vs. SJ (Oct. 24), @ CAR (Oct. 27), @ STL (Oct. 29)

6. Utah Mammoth
Previous ranking: 4

Points percentage: 63.64%

Kailer Yamamoto, RW (2.32 FPPG, 95.1% available): The winger is off to a hot start with two goals and three assists in five games. Will this sizzling trend last? Absolutely not. But there's still fantasy value to mine from Yamamoto in the meanwhile, as long as he's seeing valuable minutes alongside Barrett Hayton and Anders Lee 5-on-5 and with the extra skater.

Next seven days: vs. TB (Oct. 24), vs. MIN (Oct. 27), @ PIT (Oct. 29)

7. New York Rangers
Previous ranking: 5

Points percentage: 62.5%

Gabe Perreault, RW (1.75 FPPG, 65.9% available): Perreault has settled in with Mika Zibanejad and Alexis Lafreniere, and the trio has yet to be scored on at 5-on-5 (4-0 in 96 minutes together). He's at 1.88 FPPG over his past 10 games and is still available in about two-thirds of leagues.

Next seven days: @ OTT (Oct. 24), vs. LA (Oct. 26)

8. Minnesota Wild
Previous ranking: 8

Points percentage: 63.64%

Jared Spurgeon, D (2.40 FPPG lately, 72.8% available): Expected to make his return soon, Spurgeon once again projects to fill a prominent role on a blue line that's missing Brock Faber for the foreseeable future. Before suffering an upper-body injury, the veteran defender punched out five points, seven shots, and 14 blocked shots in six contests.

Next seven days: @ SEA (Oct. 24), @ VAN (Oct. 25), @ UTA (Oct. 27), vs. NYI (Oct. 29)

9. Ottawa Senators
Previous ranking: 12

Points percentage: 63.64%

stories.headline: St. Louis GK Bürki stretchered off after collision in Open Cup final
stories.summary: St. Louis goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head during the U.S. Open Cup final against the Columbus Crew.
stories.body:
St. Louis City goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head in a collision during his team's U.S. Open Cup final win over the Columbus Crew on Wednesday night.

In an attempt to make a save in the 70th minute, Bürki took a knee to the head from Crew winger Anass Zaroury. He remained on the ground to receive medical attention before being stretchered off the field.

Bürki was able to wave to supporters as he was taken away from the pitch. St. Louis confirmed to ESPN that Bürki was conscious and moving all extremities on his way to the hospital.

"He is currently alert and in good spirits. The club's medical staff will continue to monitor his condition and the team will provide additional updates as they become available," the club later said in a statement on X.

The score was tied 0-0 at the time of the injury, but St. Louis went on to win the game in a shootout after Burki's backup Ben Lundt made a save to help his team beat the Crew 5-3 on spot kicks.

The win earned St. Louis, which began play in MLS in 2023, its first trophy in club history.

St. Louis City captain Bürki had 43 touches and three crucial saves before the injury. He played an integral role in maintaining the 0-0 draw before being replaced by Lundt after the head injury.

Bürki, who joined St. Louis from Borussia Dortmund in 2022, stopped a corner kick from Brais Méndez that appeared to be goalbound and a flurry of other shots just before sustaining his injury.

Eleven minutes of injury time was added due to Bürki's injury, but neither team scored before the end of regulation despite Columbus outshooting St. Louis 16-3, so the game went to extra time and penalties.

stories.headline: Wayne Rooney: Bruno Fernandes, Man United players acting like 'babies'
stories.summary: Wayne Rooney has lambasted Manchester United's squad for acting like "babies" and urged Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez to look in the mirror.
stories.body:
Wayne Rooney has lambasted Manchester United's squad for acting like "babies" and urged Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez to look in the mirror.

Fernandes followed Martínez in producing an eye-catching post-match interview on the back of Wednesday's 4-1 defeat at Como in the Champions League.

The result increased the scrutiny on Michael Carrick, who then faced criticism from Fernandes for the game plan in Italy but Rooney has accused the current United captain and Martínez -- who pointed the finger at Jason Wilcox -- of being selfish.

Sources: Carrick to lead Man United against Bournemouth

During an appearance on "The United Stand" podcast, Rooney, who also called for the board to provide clarity regarding Carrick's future, said: "When Martínez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart. That was the start.

"We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players. The reason why is because them players don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said, but you have to take responsibility on the pitch, you have to take responsibility as a group of players and there were times when me and Sir Alex Ferguson wouldn't talk, but I'd run through a brick wall for him on the pitch.

"These players, they're selfish. They care about themselves, they don't care about their team-mates, don't care about the manager, about the staff or the fans, they care about themselves.

"If they're not getting what's right for them. They're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves. They have to look at themselves.

- Ogden: Who's to blame for Man United mess: Carrick, the players ... Ratcliffe?

- Dawson: Man United were abysmal in Como, but only Carrick who will suffer

"Bruno, he's having probably the worst run of form he's had since he's been at the club and again, it's no coincidence he's putting pressure on someone else because he doesn't want to face it.

"If he looks at himself in the mirror, if Martínez looks at himself in the mirror, all the players... they'll find what is looking back at them is them and it's not good enough."

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.

stories.headline: 'No regrets': why Kangaroos prop made switch from Tonga
stories.summary: Keaon Koloamatangi has revealed why he couldn't knock back the opportunity to represent Australia at the World Cup after previously doing the same with Tonga.
stories.body:
Keaon Koloamatangi has revealed why he couldn't knock back the opportunity to represent Australia at the World Cup after previously doing the same with Tonga.

In recent years, the international scene has mostly showcased players with multiple heritages moving across from tier-one sides such as New Zealand and Australia to play for nations such as Samoa and Tonga in particular.

Koloamatangi went the other way, switching from Tonga to Australia before last year's Ashes tour after previously representing the Mate Ma'a on 10 occasions, including the 2022 World Cup.

"I just want to experience everything. I was lucky enough to play for Tonga in the last World Cup in England," Koloamatangi said

"I think if Australia comes calling, it's not something you can turn your back on. It's probably the best team you can make, and it's something I want to look back on, knowing I always dreamt of doing it as a kid."

Koloamatangi, who will join St George Illawarra next season from South Sydney, has a deep appreciation for both nations and does not regard his choice this time as valuing one side of his heritage over the other.

The 28-year-old will play prop against Fiji at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday night as a proud Kangaroo.

"I played for Tonga, I've play Origin, and I wanted to play for all the nations that I am eligible for," he said.

"It's something I'm really proud of because I'm just as Australian as I am Tongan. I was born Australian and my dad's Tongan. For me, I just wanted to experience a World Cup in the Australian colours, and I've got a lot of great mates here too."

Koloamatangi admits it was "a tough decision" but the classy response of Tonga coach Kristian Woolf reassured him.

"I spoke to Woolfy and he was very grateful for the conversation I had with him. He was respectful and accepted my decision. I have no regrets," Koloamatangi said.

"I loved my time with Tonga, with the atmosphere they get and the crowds they get.

"They're such a small country, and seeing them on the big stage now I've been being blessed to be a part of it."

There is a chance Tonga and Australia could meet in the World Cup semi-final or final.

Tonga's 30-12 win over England in the opening round has them on track to reach the final-four.

"I watched the game last week and was so proud of how they turned up for their nation," Koloamatangi said.

"Obviously, I want Australia to win, but if we weren't to win, I'll be cheering the Tongans all the way. I wish nothing but the best for them."
